# Pre-reading {#sec-pre-reading}

If you haven't already, go through the course overview section. Read the
[syllabus](https://moduler.aau.dk/course/2024-2025/MEDMS24B5_1), especially the
part about what the course will cover and what we expect you to learn at the end
of it. Then read the learning design section in @sec-learning-design and
@sec-schedule to get an overview of what types of activities we will do during
the course as well as the reasons for them in relation to learning.

Related to the learning design, an important component of learning is repeated
exposure to a concept or skill. We want you to read through specific sections of
the material beforehand as we've found that these particular topics are often
more difficult to grasp and understand for beginners. Reading it beforehand will
give your brain some time to start processing the information, so that when you
see it again during the course, it will be easier to understand and learn.
During the course, you will read these sections again and we will explain them
verbally as well, to further reinforce the concepts.

Because our main learning outcome is **statistical litteracy**, we will use
tools like R that is the foundation for most modern statistical workflows.
Without a way to easily and quickly reproduce analyses, statistical work becomes
daunting and inefficient. Using R is the most common way to write statistical
analyses within the health sciences.

So, please read about R and how to set it up in @sec-install-programs,
@sec-r-and-rstudio, and @sec-installing-r-packages. R and its associated
computer code will be the main tool for the course. Learning how to program
requires a change in how you see and interact with your computer in profound
ways. Try not to underestimate R and what it can do for you in order to learn
quicker during this course.

Lastly, briefly read through the @sec-project-work so you are familiar with what
you will do at the end of the course. You'll be formally introduced to the
projects later, but we've found that students prefer and want to be aware
beforehand on what is expected of them during the project work.

::: callout-tip
To keep track of which sections to read, here is a list:

## Cheatsheets

RStudio provides some great
[cheatsheets](https://posit.co/resources/cheatsheets/) that are fantastic
resources and a great reference to have readily available, either on your
computer or printed out. We suggest that you download at least these following
cheatsheets and have them available either digitally or printed out during the
course, especially for when you do the exercises and team project work:

- [RStudio IDE](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/rstudio-ide.pdf)
- [Quarto](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/quarto.pdf)
- [dplyr](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/data-transformation.pdf)
- [ggplot2](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/data-visualization.pdf)

## Using AI

We provide solutions to the exercises, but a solved exercise is not the goal ---
learning is.

Use ChatGPT and other chat models responsibly. They can help you understand,
question, and explore, but they can also give you convincing nonsense.

**Do not outsource your thinking.**

The time to make mistakes, struggle, and learn from them is now --- not when you
are responsible for patients, colleagues, or decisions in the workplace.

### Examples:

**Legitimate use cases**

- Ask for an explanation of a statistical concept you do not understand.
- Ask for a hint when you are stuck rather than asking for the answer.
- Make it explain errors in R instead of generating the code.
- Compare your own solution with a suggested solution and identify where they
  differ.
- Ask the model to challenge your interpretation of a result or point out
  assumptions you may have missed.
- Use it after attempting an exercise to clarify mistakes and deepen your
  understanding.

**Poor use cases**

- Copying the solution without first attempting the exercise.
- Asking the model to solve an exercise so you can submit or reproduce the
  answer.
- Using a model's statistical reasoning without checking whether it is correct.
- Letting the model choose a statistical method you cannot explain yourself.

**Further resources on responsible use of AI**

- [AAU: Generative AI for
  students](https://www.en.aub.aau.dk/students/generative-ai) --- guidance on
  academic practice, privacy, evaluating AI, useful scenarios, prompting, and
  avoiding over-reliance on AI.
- [AAU: Rules for use of generative
  AI](https://www.studerende.aau.dk/regler-og-praktisk/regler/regler-for-brug-af-generativ-ai) ---
  know the rules that apply to your studies and exams.
- [AAU: Scenarios for using generative
  AI](https://www.en.aub.aau.dk/students/generative-ai/scenarios-for-use) ---
  examples of appropriate uses of AI for studying, understanding difficult
  material, and exam preparation.
- [UNESCO: Guidance for generative AI in education and
  research](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/guidance-generative-ai-education-and-research) ---
  a broader perspective on human-centred and responsible use of generative AI in
  education.

*You are responsible for what you submit --- and for what you learn.*
